blocks.content: provisioner "file" copies a local file or directory to the newly created resource, requiring the same real connection as remote-exec, and often paired directly with it.
1. Copying to the Resource
provisioner "file" copies a local file, or an entire directory, from the machine running Terraform, directly onto the newly created resource.
This is genuinely the simplest of the three provisioners conceptually, its entire job is moving real bytes from one place to another, nothing more.
Despite that simplicity, it shares the same genuine connection requirement as remote-exec, reaching the resource at all is still real, necessary work.
Understanding it well rounds out the complete picture of what all three provisioners can actually do, before this module turns to the honest question of when they should.
The file provisioner's narrow scope, purely moving bytes, is genuinely part of what makes it easier to reason about than remote-exec's arbitrary command execution.

blocks.content: 2. The Same connection Requirement
Exactly like remote-exec, covered in the previous topic, reaching the resource to copy a file onto it requires the same real connection block, SSH or WinRM details.
This is genuinely worth recognizing directly, the file provisioner and remote-exec share this one real requirement entirely, everything else about them differs.
If a connection has already been proven to work for remote-exec on a given resource, the file provisioner can generally reuse that exact same, already-tested configuration.
This shared requirement is precisely why the two are so often used together, covered directly later in this topic.

blocks.content: 3. source and destination
source is the real, local path on the machine running Terraform, destination is the real, remote path on the resource itself where that file should actually land.
Getting destination right genuinely matters, the target directory must already exist on the resource, the file provisioner does not create missing parent directories automatically.
source can point at a single file, or, as covered next, an entire local directory, genuinely flexible depending on what actually needs to move.
Keeping paths relative and predictable, rather than hard-coded to one specific machine, makes this configuration genuinely more portable across a real team.

4. Copying an Entire Directory
source is genuinely not limited to a single file, pointing it at a local directory copies that entire directory, recursively, onto the resource.
This is genuinely useful for a real, multi-file configuration bundle, an application's full config directory, for instance, rather than copying each file with a separate provisioner block.
The trailing slash on the source path genuinely matters here, affecting whether the directory itself, or just its contents, land at the destination.
Testing this behavior once, deliberately, on a real, disposable resource is worth the small upfront effort before relying on it in a real, shared configuration.

blocks.content: 5. A Real Use Case: Configuration Files
blocks.text: 5. A Real Use Case: Configuration Files

blocks.content: Copying a real configuration file, or a setup script itself, onto a new instance right after creation is the clearest, most common real use of this provisioner.
This use case connects directly back to the file structure conventions covered in the HCL module, a clean, well-organized local config directory copies cleanly onto the resource.
Keeping the source files themselves under real version control, alongside the rest of the Terraform configuration, is a genuinely good, common practice.
That way, a change to the deployed configuration is genuinely visible and reviewable, exactly like any other change to the codebase.

blocks.content: 6. Often Paired With Remote-Exec
A genuinely common real pattern pairs the two, file copies a script onto the new resource first, and remote-exec then runs it, together forming a complete, real bootstrapping step.
This pairing genuinely plays to each provisioner's specific strength, file moves real bytes reliably, remote-exec then executes real logic against them.
Ordering matters here, Terraform runs provisioners in the order they are declared, so the file copy genuinely needs to be declared before the remote-exec that depends on it.
This exact pairing is one of the most common real, practical patterns anyone using provisioners at all is likely to encounter.

blocks.content: 7. A Real, Honest Follow-Up: Permissions
Files copied this way land with whatever real permissions the transfer mechanism defaults to, often still needing an explicit chmod afterward, exactly why the pairing above includes one.
This is a genuinely easy detail to overlook the first time, a script copied but not marked executable simply fails to run, with an error that is not always immediately obvious.
Building the permission fix directly into the paired remote-exec block, as shown above, keeps this handled consistently, rather than relying on it being remembered separately each time.
For anything beyond a script, real ownership, not just executability, may also genuinely need adjusting depending on which user the destination service actually runs as.

blocks.content: 8. A Real Limitation Worth Knowing
The file provisioner has no real way to verify the destination directory already exists, a missing parent directory on the resource genuinely causes the whole copy to fail.
This is worth testing deliberately against a real, fresh resource rather than assuming a destination path will simply work because it looks correct on paper.
If the destination directory is not guaranteed to already exist, a preceding remote-exec step creating it first is a genuinely reasonable, real fix.
Being aware of this limitation upfront avoids a confusing, real failure that has nothing to do with the file content itself.

9. Preferring This Over Inline File Contents
blocks.text: 9. Preferring This Over Inline File Contents

blocks.content: It is genuinely worth preferring the file provisioner over embedding large file contents directly inside a remote-exec inline command as an echoed string.
Inline-embedded file contents are genuinely harder to read, harder to review, and harder to keep in sync with the real, actual file elsewhere in a repository.
Keeping real file content in its own real file, copied over cleanly with this provisioner, is simply the more maintainable, honest choice in nearly every real case.
This small, practical preference reflects the same underlying philosophy the rest of this module builds toward, real, deliberate, well-understood choices over convenient shortcuts.

With all three provisioners now covered individually, comparing them directly side by side makes their real, distinct roles genuinely clear.
local-exec runs locally, with no connection requirement at all, remote-exec and file both require a real connection, but serve genuinely different real purposes once connected.
Recognizing which of the three actually fits a given real situation is precisely the skill the next topic in this module builds on directly.

points: The file provisioner copies a local file or directory onto the newly created resource, requiring the same real connection block as remote-exec.
source is the local path, destination is the remote path, an entire directory can genuinely be copied, not just a single file.
